newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices drop further, cocoa at 8-year high.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices drop further, cocoa at 8-year high.

text.p: Coffee prices fell sharply on Friday ahead of a report by the U.S. Agriculture Department on the size of the coffee crop in Brazil, the top world producer.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery ended 12.10 cents a pound lower at 195.70 cents. That compares to a 20-year high price of 318 cents seen on May 29.

The Agriculture Department report, released after the futures market closed, stunned many coffee traders by projecting Brazil's harvest at 28 million 132-pound bags, up from 27.5 million a year earlier.
The estimate compares with the Brazilian government's current projection of a 22 million bag crop and coffee trade estimates of 23 to 25 million bags.

"What is the most shocking thing is to say there is more coming this year than last. That is totally wrong," Jorge Esteve, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters Association, told Reuters in Rio de Janeiro.
"It's certainly not what we expect. It's too high," said John Wolthers of Brazilian coffee export firm Icatu/Sumatra.
The department also forecast world coffee production in the 1997/98 year to match the 1991/92 record of 103.7 million bags, compared with 100.7 million bags the previous season.

"That is negative," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "At 103.7 million, you're looking at a stock build. Those people who were looking for $4 are probably going to be looking at $1.50 soon," Platt said of futures prices.

Coffee prices have risen from around 90 cents a pound in December on very tight stockpiles at roasters and the outlook for smaller supplies this year, a conclusion that Friday's estimates call into question.

Cocoa prices shot to the highest level in eight years as professional fund speculators bought on concerns about next season's crop in top producer Ivory Coast and worries about crop problems from El Nino, a developing weather pattern.
September cocoa closed $61 higher at $1,632 a metric ton.
The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said ocean temperatures in the South Pacific were the highest since August 1983, with an El Nino effect in progress.
In the past, dryness in the southern hemisphere has been one result of El Nino. The 1983 El Nino caused severe drought in Indonesia, the world's third-largest cocoa producer.

"El Nino is a factor that affects areas where cocoa is grown, and it is starting," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "I may not have an immediate effect, but there will eventually be less cocoa because of it.
Underpinning the rally has also been a worry that dry weather in Ivory Coast may be hampering early pod development for the coming 1997/98 cocoa crop, traders said.
"It's the new bull for the minute," said Allendale Inc market analyst Jim Cordier. "The funds are ready to throw their money in another soft besides coffee."
At the Chicago Board of Trade, excellent growing weather in the Midwest generally kept a cap on grain prices.
But lingering concerns about low U.S. soybean stocks boosted that market despite this week's Agriculture Department estimate for a record 2.6 billion bushel crop this year.
Soybeans for July delivery closed up 13 cents a bushel at $8.54-1/2, while July wheat closed down 1/2 cent a bushel at $3.52-1/2 and July corn up 1/4 cent a bushel at $2.71-1/2.
Soybean supplies remain near 20-year lows even after the Agriculture Department raised its estimate for remaining stockpiles this September by 5 million bushels to 130 million.

"It's still tight, there's no question about that," said Sid Love, an analyst with Kropf and Love Consulting in Overland Park, Kan. "If the USDA hadn't raised imports, the carryout would have been 115 (million) bushels."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil for July delivery closed 14 cents higher at $18.83 a barrel as chart-watching speculators led the mostly technical trade.

"The bears would like to see $18.50 obliterated once and for all to give further impetus to the downside move. For the bulls it has been a very difficult week," said Andrew Lebow, an energy futures trader for E.D. & F. Man International Inc.

Crude futures were influenced for several days by comments by various sources suggesting a renewed Iraqi "oil-for-food" deal might be hung up because Baghdad wanted to make a political protest about the tough process of approving the purchase and distribution of goods under the scheme.
But Iraq's envoy to the United Nations on Friday made it clear that Baghdad did not intend to hold up oil sales.

Though neither the Iraqi diplomat nor U.N. officials involved in the deal could give a time for the restart of Iraqi crude exports, both said the process was proceeding as expected and without any political obstacles.
"This whole Iraqi thing has just given rationalization to moves. The psychology of the market is still bearish," said Lebow.
Refined oil products followed crude, with July gasoline up 0.32 cent at 57.40 cents a gallon and July heating oil up 0.02 cent at 51.64 cents a gallon.
